deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics: no formulas, computations or derivations. It is a set of reading excerpts and notes in German, continuing the Herbart excerpts on the previous page (Plato, Aristotle, matter and form, the 'contradiction in change').

(1) The page opens by finishing a sentence from the previous page ('...dem Räumlichen setzen konnten'). It then quotes Herbart: the ancient philosophers could not accept that mathematical constructions and general concepts are merely products of our representing (Vorstellen). 'It lacked psychology.'

(2) Mathematical objects took a long time to reach their proper place, and have barely reached it now. Clarke still made space an attribute of the infinite Being (the Clarke–Leibniz correspondence). Kant opens the Transcendental Aesthetic by asking what space and time are. Are they real beings? Are they only determinations or relations of things that would belong to things in themselves even if not intuited? This is a paraphrase of KrV A23/B37.

(3) A heading follows: 'Über die ... der Psychologie unter die ontologischen Begriffe', with the reference '1838. W. VII. 175'. This is Herbart, Werke (ed. Hartenstein), vol. VII, p. 175, a late (1838) piece. The excerpt runs as follows.
- Once ontology, after examining the 'I' and rejecting idealism, has supplied psychology with the concept of the Real, two subsumptions follow. The soul-substrate's Real falls under the ontological concept of the Real. The simple sensation, from which representations are later explained, falls under 'self-preservation' (Selbsterhaltung).
- If psychology then proceeds to its mathematical investigations, there remains room for a further thought. In a Real of whatever kind, a plurality of opposed states might exist, and one may ask what follows from this.
- This is Herbart's programme of a mathematical psychology of inhibiting representations, stated here only programmatically.

(4) Under a sub-heading ('... von der ontologischen Seite', S. 176), Herbart says the main character of his system is the strict separation of pure Being from actual Happening (Geschehen). There are known systems that treat pure Being as if Happening were already contained in it. A counterpart would treat Happening as if it licensed the inferences others draw from Being. Metaphysics would then stand between two systems and must guard against both. The extremes touch, so the mixing of Being and Happening would return by the other route.

(5) Final heading 'Raum (Materie)'. It notes that Herbart's treatment of space in the Allgemeine Metaphysik II was conditioned by Leibniz's Theoria motus abstracti (Opera, ed. Dutens, II, 2, p. 35).

The lower third of the page is blank apart from mirror-image bleed-through of the English Locke excerpts (Essay II.21) from the next page.

No mathematical problem is served. The notes document Riemann's study of Herbart's metaphysics and psychology and of the philosophical status of space, which forms background to his Naturphilosophie fragments and the Habilitationsvortrag.

deep.surprise_reason: The page consists purely of reading excerpts from Herbart, with a reference to Leibniz. Riemann's close study of Herbart is well documented, both in the Naturphilosophie fragments in the Werke and in the secondary literature (e.g. Scholz, Ferreirós). There is no mathematics and no original result.
transcription_corrections: The heading word read as 'Unterordnung[?]' is uncertain in the image; it may be 'Stellung'. The construction 'der Psychologie unter die ontologischen Begriffe' is clear.
'Entfernung[?] von der ontologischen Seite' is doubtful; the word looks more like 'Betrachtung' or 'Beleuchtung'.
'Die Metaphysik könnte[?] alsdann in die Mitte' likely reads 'Die Metaphysik stände alsdann in der Mitte', which the syntax requires.
'S.176' is written in the left margin as a page reference to the same Herbart volume (W. VII).

'[-Im Begriff mit-]' is a struck-out false start before 'die Darstellung in der Allg. Met. II'. The abbreviation is most likely 'Allg. Met.' (Herbart's Allgemeine Metaphysik, Part II), not 'Allg. M. u. Met.'.
The faint mirrored English text in the lower half of the page is bleed-through of the Locke excerpts on the following page, not content of this page.
